transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-22
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Lucas Ortiz (Redwood SE), Priya Narang (BlueHarbor Infra), Tom Bowers (BlueHarbor Platform), Elena Ruiz (BlueHarbor Security)

Auto-summary: quick recap at end; slides referenced: 'redwood-private-networking.pdf' and 'kv-batching-benchmarks.xlsx' (links shared in chat)

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we have about an hour, we wanted to walk through the private vpc net topology and then drill into runtime behavior when your traffic needs to hairpin back to the same VPC for KV cache hits.
[00:18] Priya: thanks, Maya. Our team is basically trying to understand whether PrivateLink is sufficient or we need transit gateway. Also, we have strict egress rules - only specific NATs allowed, and egress must go through an egress proxy for logging.
[00:36] Lucas: totally. We'll cover both options. Quick note: in Redwood Private we run the control plane in your VPC for private deployments, and the inference nodes sit in a dedicated subnet inside customer account — so networking is pretty configurable.
[00:49] Tom: a quick network detail — our subnets are 3 AZs, each AZ has a pair of NAT gateways in private mode, and we lock down route tables. We also use internal DNS resolvers with split-horizon for service discovery.
[01:05] Elena: security: SOC2 ok, but we need to see audit-log flow, KMS integration for keys, and if HSM is required. Also, can you prove that plaintext tokens don't leave our VPC?
[01:20] Maya: yes, for Private deployments the tokenized payload stays in your VPC. Control plane is private; data path can be pinned to dedicated capacity. We'll share KMS integration docs.
[01:32] Lucas: jumping into the runtime side — the main runtime concerns are latency SLOs when KV cache is enabled, because KV lookups for past prefix tokens sometimes go to a cache service that might be in the same subnet or cross-AZ, depending on config.
[01:49] Priya: can you clarify hairpinning? Our infra team is worried about cross-subnet calls that egress then re-ingress, adding NAT costs and latency.
[02:02] Lucas: right, hairpin occurs if your routing forces packets to leave the AZ/subnet and come back. Two common patterns we see: (1) PrivateLink endpoint service where queries stay internal via endpoint interfaces in each AZ — minimal hairpin, or (2) Transit gateway / centralized NAT where you might see hairpin if the route table points out.
[02:24] Tom: ok, so PrivateLink seems better for avoiding hairpin, but we also need centralized egress logging which sits outside the VPC. That would force egress to a proxy — how does that affect the KV cache p95?
[02:40] Lucas: in our internal testing with batch sizes of 8 and quantized int8 models, adding an egress proxy in the path increased p95 for short responses by about 22-35ms depending on proxy latency. For larger sequences the overhead is amortized across tokens. We can share the bench spreadsheet.
[02:58] Priya: that's useful. What about batching? Can we control batching window to keep p95 tight for interactive queries?
[03:08] Lucas: yes, Redwood's runtime supports dynamic batching policies. You can set a max latency window (e.g., 20ms), target batch sizes, and preferential routing for latency-critical traffic to dedicated pools. There's a tradeoff: smaller windows reduce batching benefit and increase per-token cost.
[03:27] Elena: what about quantization modes? We saw a note about 4-bit quantization — is that production-ready? Any accuracy regressions?
[03:35] Lucas: good question. We support int8 and 4-bit quant (LLM.int4 style) on certain backends. Int8 gives a smaller perf gain but is generally safer for quality. 4-bit can reduce memory and increase throughput by ~1.6x in our tests but you should run eval sets — we can attach quality diffs from your eval.
[03:55] Tom: re: KV cache — is the cache colocated with model servers or a separate service?
[04:01] Maya: it can be either. For best latency, we recommend colocating KV cache in the same subnet/AZ as the model replicas. If customers centralize cache for dedupe across pools you might see cross-AZ reads.
[04:15] Lucas: and to add, we have an option for local in-memory prefix cache on the inference node plus a backing distributed KV store. That gives a tiny hit when misses occur.
[04:28] Priya: how do DNS and resolver settings play here? We use a private resolver that blocks external names; do endpoints resolve via interface IPs or DNS names?
[04:39] Lucas: PrivateLink endpoint interfaces present ENI IPs in your subnet; we recommend using IPs in route/nat config or creating internal DNS CNAMEs to those ENIs. If your resolver blocks external names, ensure the VPC DNS and hostfile mapping are in place.
[04:56] Tom: any gotchas with NACLs or security groups?
[05:00] Lucas: yes, NACLs that are too strict can drop ephemeral ports used by gRPC or streaming. Security groups should allow TLS on the configured ports between model nodes and cache endpoints; PrivateLink uses ENI so traffic is intra-VPC and respects SGs.
[05:15] Priya: in the worst case, say our topology forces a hairpin via central NAT, can Redwood detect and suggest a fix?
[05:23] Lucas: we have network diagnostics in the console that show observed RTTs and flagged hairpin paths by looking at traceroutes and packet timing. We can also suggest creating interface endpoints per AZ or updating route tables.
[05:38] Elena: about audit logs: can logs be exported to our S3 bucket and forwarded to SIEM without leaving VPC?
[05:46] Maya: yes, for Private deploys we can push audit logs to your bucket or Kinesis inside the VPC. We support KMS CMKs for encryption; HSM can be arranged as an enterprise add-on.
[05:59] Tom: let's talk throughput: we anticipate peak 250 concurrent streams at short bursts, average 90 qps, mostly short prompts (<=128 tokens). What bucket sizes and GPU counts should we provision?
[06:13] Lucas: for that profile with batching window 20-30ms and quantized int8, a single T4-class pool can handle about 80-120 concurrent short streams depending on model. For 250 peaks I'd recommend dedicated pool across 3 GPUs with autoscale and pre-warmed replicas, or reserved capacity of 4-6 GPUs to keep headroom. Exact numbers depend on model and quantization.
[06:36] Priya: does PrivateLink add per-request overhead?
[06:40] Lucas: negligible if you're in the same AZ — typically 1-3ms. Cross-AZ PrivateLink traffic is routed through the provider's networking and can add more.
[06:50] Tom: are there scenarios where transit gateway is preferred?
[06:53] Lucas: transit gateway is useful when you need connectivity across many VPCs or centralized egress. But for low-latency inference with per-AZ replicas, PrivateLink with per-AZ endpoints is lower lat and avoids hairpin. Transit gateway can be fine if you accept a small latency increase and want simpler centralized management.
[07:10] Priya: training vs inference — irrelevant here, but does the runtime need special MTU tuning? We saw packet fragmentation in another vendor.
[07:19] Lucas: yes, MTU mismatches can cause fragmentation and slowdowns for large payloads. We recommend aligning MTU across ENIs, load balancers, and any on-prem VPN. Also check the jumbo frame settings if you have high throughput between datacenters.
[07:32] (brief pause)
[07:38] Maya: we've dropped a link to the 'redwood-private-networking.pdf' in the chat, it contains example CloudFormation/Terraform snippets for PrivateLink and Route Table entries.
[07:47] Tom: great, we'll pull that.
[07:50] Priya: quick-ish question: if we pin requests to dedicated capacity, do logs and metrics still go to Redwood console outside our VPC?
[07:59] Maya: metrics can be routed to your Prometheus/Grafana in VPC or mirrored to Redwood console depending on configuration. For Private deployments you can choose to keep telemetry in VPC and only export aggregated metrics.
[08:13] Elena: we need to confirm retention periods on logs for compliance.
[08:17] Maya: noted, we'll include that in the security pack we share.
[08:22] Lucas: switching to bench numbers — we ran a micro-benchmark: model X with int8 quant, batch 4, window 25ms, p95 was 145ms without egress proxy, and 180ms when routed through proxy adding ~28-35ms. With batch 8 p95 dropped to 120ms but cold-start variance increased.
[08:46] Tom: cold starts — how do you minimize them?
[08:49] Lucas: keep warm replicas, use pre-warm hooks, and configure startup concurrency. Also, use model warm cache on nodes; the KV prefix cache helps reduce model recompute for repeated prompts.
[09:02] Priya: about KV — is invalidation deterministic? We want predictable TTLs across nodes.
[09:08] Lucas: TTLs are configurable and invalidation events can be broadcast through our control plane; but if you centralize cache you should set consistent TTL and eviction policy to avoid staleness.
[09:20] Priya: how do we test for hairpin?
[09:24] Lucas: we can run a traceroute script from a test instance in each subnet and show the path to the cache endpoint; we also have a synthetic load tool that simulates inference traffic and flags cross-AZ hops. We'll give you the scripts.
[09:39] Maya: quick interjection, we should recap the two suggested architectures: 1) Per-AZ PrivateLink endpoints + local KV caches for low-latency; 2) Centralized cache behind transit gateway + egress proxy for centralized logging. Each has tradeoffs.
[09:56] Tom: and security wise both can be fine with proper SGs, NACLs, KMS.
[10:01] Elena: what about cost implications of more ENIs/PrivateLink endpoints?
[10:05] Maya: there is some ENI and endpoint-hour cost plus data processing charges on the provider side, but often the performance gains offset cross-AZ egress and NAT costs. We'll produce a rough TCO comparison for you.
[10:17] Priya: can Redwood's runtime recognize and prefer local KV caches?
[10:22] Lucas: yes, we have a locality-aware routing policy. If there's a local cache in the same AZ it prefers that; fallback is global cache with configurable timeouts. That avoids unnecessary cross-AZ reads.
[10:35] Tom: do you support endpoint policies to restrict which principals can call the PrivateLink endpoint?
[10:39] Maya: yes, endpoint policies and SG rules are supported. We can show a policy template in the doc.
[10:46] (background noise, someone shuffling papers)
[10:54] Priya: one more nit: our egress proxy does TLS inspection, which re-terminates TLS. That might interfere with end-to-end TLS expectations.
[11:03] Lucas: if you're doing TLS inspection you will break mutual TLS; we recommend terminating at your proxy and then re-mtls to internal endpoints, or we can configure TLS to be internal-only with cert rotation via your KMS.
[11:19] Elena: do you have an HSM integration playbook?
[11:23] Maya: yes, enterprise pack. We'll attach HSM/KMS integration doc and an audit schema.
[11:30] Tom: ok, let's surface a concrete performance acceptance criteria: p95 <= 200ms for short prompts under typical batch config, and no more than 30ms added by our egress proxy. Reasonable?
[11:43] Lucas: that's reasonable as a starting SLO. We'll run the staging tests and report p50/p95/p99 and the distribution.
[11:51] Priya: what's the recommended test harness?
[11:54] Lucas: we'll give you our load generator YAML — it simulates variable inter-arrival times, batching window, and token lengths; it also captures traceroutes and per-hop timings.
[12:06] (crosstalk)
[12:12] Maya: ok I'll recap next steps — share network diagram, PrivateLink and SG snippets, bench results and KV telemetry, and the test harness. We'll reconvene after you run the staging harness.
[12:22] Tom: perfect. Thanks, everyone.
[12:25] Elena: thanks.
[12:27] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional words garbled (e.g., 'kv cash', 'pre-warm' transcribed as 'prewarm'), speaker assignments may be approximate. Links shared in chat: redwood-private-networking.pdf, kv-batching-benchmarks.xlsx, network-tracer-scripts.tar.gz
